paras: The reported lynching of Dick Ellison was the death of a Black youth found dead between Hot Springs and Malvern, Arkansas, in October 1881, as reported in a dispatch dated October 14. The dispatch supposed that the dead youth was Dick Ellison, accused of attempting to outrage Mrs. Jacob Parker, and concluded that he had been caught and lynched by a pursuing posse. The item ran in at least seven newspapers within two days, but the identification and the lynching both rested on inference.

According to the dispatch, Ellison was accused of attempting to outrage Mrs. Jacob Parker and had escaped, with a posse in pursuit. The papers give no date, place or details for the alleged attempt itself.

A report reached Hot Springs that "a negro boy was found dead between here and Malvern," whom it described as "supposed to be Dick Ellison." From the discovery the dispatch reasoned that he "must have fallen into the hands of the pursuing posse and been lynched," while the St. Paul version spoke only of "his pursuers." No cause of death, witness, place of seizure or method of killing is reported.

No report of an inquest, a confirmed identification, or any arrest in Ellison's death appears in the coverage. The same St. Louis dispatch also reported the jailing at Hot Springs of three men charged with assassinating Frank Pollick, a separate case.

The story reached the press as a St. Louis special from Hot Springs, first in the Memphis Public Ledger on October 14 under the subhead "The Remains of a Would-Be Outrager Found." On October 15 the Savannah Morning News headed it "Negro Lynched," stating as fact what the text presented as supposition. Other editors hedged: the St. Paul Daily Globe used "Probably Lynched" and the Memphis Daily Appeal "A Supposed Lynching."

In Richmond, Wheeling and Knoxville the item ran as routine telegraph news under headings such as "Crime in Arkansas" and "Terse Telegrams." The copies differ only in small details, spelling the accuser's name Parker or Park, and the Wheeling paper garbled the location as "between St. Louis and Malvern." None of the papers described the youth by more than his race and the accusation, and no follow-up report appears in the coverage.

reader.title: Reported lynching of Dick Ellison
bases: Every copy reports a Black youth found dead after fleeing an accusation of attempted outrage, presumed to have been 'lynched' by a pursuing posse (A1, A2, A3).

A body was reported found (A1), but the identification was only 'supposed' and the lynching by a posse was the dispatch's inference ('must have fallen into the hands of'), with no reported cause of death, witness, or inquest (A1, A3, A4); the papers do not establish who killed him or how.
All seven copies reproduce one Hot Springs report relayed through St. Louis, with near-identical wording (A1, A2, A5); no local, follow-up, or independent account was found.

accounts.label: Hot Springs report via St. Louis wire
accounts.gist: A negro boy was found dead between Hot Springs and Malvern, supposed to be Dick Ellison, who had escaped after an alleged attempted outrage and who 'must have' been caught and lynched by the pursuing posse.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed the item 'Negro Lynched', treating the inference as fact, while the Memphis Public Ledger called him a 'Would-Be Outrager'.
The St. Paul Daily Globe ('Probably Lynched') and Memphis Daily Appeal ('A Supposed Lynching') hedged the headline.
Richmond, Wheeling and Knoxville papers ran it as routine telegraph news ('Crime in Arkansas', 'Terse Telegrams', 'Arkansas News').

conflicts.note: The Wheeling version is evidently a garble of the St. Louis-relayed wire; every other copy has Hot Springs.
Spelling variant within the same wire.
